idiom_name: small Node interface + []Node child slice, child management on the concrete container
implementation_notes: Go does not need the GoF class hierarchy: a small interface declaring only the operations that are meaningful for every node, plus concrete structs whose container type holds a []Node slice and delegates recursively, reproduces the pattern with far less ceremony. Keep Add/Remove off the interface - leaves cannot honestly implement them - and put child management on the container type that actually owns the slice. The standard library ships the pattern twice and is the shape to imitate: go/ast (ast.Node implemented by leaf and container nodes, traversed by ast.Inspect/PreorderStack) and io/fs (FS/DirEntry walked by fs.WalkDir). Choose a Walk/visitor method when there are many algorithms and few node kinds, methods on the interface when the opposite holds.
pitfalls: Putting Add/Remove/Children on the component interface forces leaves into stub methods and turns a compile error into a runtime surprise; keep container-only operations on the container type.
A nil entry in a []Node compiles fine and panics on the first traversal - validate inside Add.
Mutating the children slice while walking it changes or skips elements; iterate over a copy whenever the operation may add or remove nodes.
